The inclusion–exclusion principle

To count the elements in a union of overlapping sets, adding the set sizes overcounts everything in an overlap. The inclusion–exclusion principle corrects this systematically: subtract the pairwise overlaps, then add back the elements in all three sets (which were subtracted once too often). This calculator applies it for two or three sets, fills in every region of the Venn diagram and checks that your numbers are consistent.

Try changing the input

Make |A ∩ B| larger than |A|. The calculator rejects it: an overlap can never contain more elements than either set it belongs to.

Formulas

∣A∪B∣=∣A∣+∣B∣−∣A∩B∣
∣A∪B∪C∣=∣A∣+∣B∣+∣C∣−∣A∩B∣−∣A∩C∣−∣B∩C∣+∣A∩B∩C∣

If the total ∣U∣ is known, the number of elements in none of the sets is ∣U∣−∣A∪B∪C∣. Regions such as "only A" are found by subtracting: ∣A∣−∣A∩B∣−∣A∩C∣+∣A∩B∩C∣.

Worked example

How many numbers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2, 3 or 5?

Step 1 — Set sizes

∣A∣=50 (multiples of 2), ∣B∣=33 (of 3), ∣C∣=20 (of 5).

Step 2 — Overlaps

Multiples of 6: 16; of 10: 10; of 15: 6; of 30: 3.

Step 3 — Inclusion–exclusion

50+33+20−16−10−6+3=74

So 74 numbers are divisible by at least one of 2, 3, 5, and 26 by none of them.

Assumptions and checks

  • Supported: two or three finite sets with whole-number counts.
  • Every Venn region must contain 0 or more elements; otherwise the counts are contradictory and no result is shown.
  • The total ∣U∣ is optional; if given, it must be at least the size of the union.
